analysis.one_liner: Bans banks from forcing victims of unauthorized account fraud into arbitration.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: referred to the House Financial Services Committee in December 2016, it sat there until the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After the Wells Fargo scandal, in which employees opened millions of accounts customers never asked for, courts still forced those customers to settle their fraud claims in private arbitration because they had signed arbitration clauses attached to their real accounts. This bill would make those clauses unenforceable for any dispute involving a credit card or bank account the consumer never applied for, restoring the right to sue in court. It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and died there without a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers whose identities were used to open accounts without their consent. Instead of being pushed into arbitration under clauses they never knowingly agreed to for those accounts, they could sue for fraud in a public court, where proceedings are on the record, results are precedential, and class actions are possible.

how_it_helps.text: No predispute arbitration agreement would be valid or enforceable in a dispute involving a credit card that was not issued in response to a request or application for that card.
The same ban applies to personal bank accounts — demand deposits, savings, and similar asset accounts — that the consumer did not request, with trust accounts carved out.

The bill's findings document the problem it targets: the consumer bureau found Wells Fargo opened as many as 1,534,280 checking accounts and 565,443 credit cards without customers' knowledge or consent between May 2011 and July 2015, and courts nonetheless bound those customers to arbitration clauses.
The findings note consumers have no meaningful choice whether to submit claims to arbitration and are typically unaware they have given up their right to sue in court.

analysis.who_pays: Banks and credit card issuers that rely on mandatory arbitration clauses. They would face courtroom fraud claims — including class actions — over accounts opened without customer consent, with the legal costs and public exposure that come with litigation.

drawbacks.text: The bill is deliberately narrow: it only strips arbitration clauses when the account itself was never requested. Fraud disputes tied to accounts the consumer did open would still be forced into arbitration, so a large share of the problem described in the bill's own findings — customers of legitimate Wells Fargo accounts bound to arbitration over fake-account fraud — may remain.

The standard industry objection to arbitration limits is that courtroom litigation, especially class actions, is slower and more expensive, and that those costs are ultimately passed to all customers through higher fees; arbitration can resolve individual disputes faster and at lower cost to the consumer.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but scoped tightly: it restores the courtroom only for victims of accounts they never asked for, which is where consent to arbitration is most plainly absent. The main honest criticism is that it does so little — leaving arbitration clauses fully intact everywhere else — which makes the industry cost argument modest as well. On balance a targeted consumer-rights fix whose main drawback is its own narrowness.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended three weeks later.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on December 1, 2016, with 14 Democratic cosponsors, and referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.
The complete action history shows only two steps: introduction and the committee referral. No hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled.
The 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, so the bill died in committee and would have needed to be reintroduced to move again.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks and card issuers are better off: their arbitration clauses remain fully enforceable, and fraud claims over unauthorized accounts stay in private arbitration with no public record and no class actions.

for.name: Rep. Brad Sherman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in response to the Wells Fargo unauthorized-accounts scandal, with findings drawn from the consumer bureau's enforcement action.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

against.name: Rep. Jeb Hensarling
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee of referral, never brought the bill to a markup or moved it toward the floor.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 supporters — the sponsor and 14 cosponsors — were Democrats, and the Republican-controlled Financial Services Committee never acted on it; no Republican is on record either way.

industries.note: The bill would strip their ability to force fraud claims over unauthorized accounts into arbitration, exposing them to courtroom litigation and class actions. Arbitration clauses limit the cost, publicity, and scale of consumer fraud claims.

industries.industry: Arbitration providers and the consumer-claims defense system built on mandatory arbitration
industries.note: A narrower market for consumer dispute arbitration in credit card and deposit accounts. The loss is marginal because the ban covers only accounts the consumer never requested.

Fraud victims could again sue in court, which is where class actions and public judgments are possible. Their gain is the public's gain here: the same proceeding that pays the lawyer can return money to defrauded account holders.
